title: What liana wood tells us: a commentary on ‘Are differences in xylem vessel traits and their geographical variation among liana species related to the distribution patterns of climbing mechanisms in a temperate zone?’
content: Lianas are non-self-supporting woody vines that have thin stems and use upright host trees to ascend to the forest canopy. They use various climbing mechanisms to attach to the host trees such as twining, tendrils, scrambling and root climbing (Dias et al., 2024, Fig. 1A). These climbing mechanisms are expected to influence how the liana branches extend, and the resultant plant growth and life forms. However, few studies have addressed the impacts of these climbing mechanisms on the ecology of lianas. Kusakabe et al. (2023)found that, although liana abundance decreases in colder regions at high latitude and altitude (Schnitzer, 2005), the extent of the decrease depended on the climbing mechanism; the abundance of twining climbers decreased, but the abundance of root climbers increased with increasing latitude. These previous studies have suggested that freeze–thaw-induced embolism (hereafter FT embolism) is a key stress leading to a decline in liana abundance (Schnitzer, 2005; Lobos-Catalán and Jiménez-Castillo, 2023). FT embolism involves inhibition of water transport in stem xylem due to filling of the vessel lumen with gases that appear during freezing and thawing of xylem sap in winter. As xylem dysfunction by FT embolism has more serious effects in stem wood with wider vessels (Davis et al., 1999), liana species with wide vessels are not expected to be found in cold regions where freeze–thaw events frequently occur. In this issue of Annals of Botany, Kusakabe et al. (2025) hypothesize that root climbers have narrower vessels and populations of twining species growing at colder sites also have narrower vessels to maintain stem water transport against FT embolism. They surveyed over 13000 sections of stem wood from eight liana species, including three twining, one tendril and four root climbers, and revealed several new aspects of liana ecology.
